title: At the end of life
hookLine: Pure Land practice at the deathbed: the name said with the dying

lines: A HOSPITAL ROOM, LATE AT NIGHT.
cards: A hospital room, late at night. An old woman lies still, her breathing slow and shallow. Around the bed, her family and a few friends from the temple stand close, chanting softly, steadily: Amituofo, Amituofo.
When one voice tires, another picks it up. She may not be able to speak anymore, or even open her eyes. But the name keeps going, just above her, like a handrail she can reach for in the dark.
Today: at the end of life.

teach.h: A GOOD FRIEND AT THE BEDSIDE.
teach.b: First, the root, from a week ago: in the Contemplation Sutra, a dying man too pressed by pain to picture anything, and a good friend at his side who tells him to just say the name.
Some Pure Land teachers trace deathbed practice to that friend. The point isn't only what the dying person can do. It's who is sitting with them.

Chanting the name with and for the dying has its own name, zhunian, helping recitation. People take turns, so the name never stops, and the dying person can follow it with their mind even without the breath to say it.

Tradition says the monk Genshin, in his book on birth in the Pure Land, described deathbed rites: an image of Amida set facing west, and colored threads tied from the image's hand to the hand of the dying, a thread to hold on the way.

teach.h: SETTLED IN LIFE, OR AT THE LAST BREATH.
teach.b: For Shinran, birth in the Pure Land is settled in this life, the moment shinjin is given. So in Shin Buddhism the last hour is not a test, and there's no need to wait anxiously for Amida to come at death.
Other Pure Land communities place great weight on the deathbed and the last thought of the name. Both do the same simple thing for the person in the bed: they don't leave them alone with the dark.

how: In Chinese Pure Land communities, family and temple members take turns chanting Amitabha's name at the bedside of the dying; Japanese Pure Land traditions have their own deathbed rites, and in Shin Buddhism, where birth is understood as settled in life, the nembutsu is said at the end in gratitude.

games.q: what does “at the end of life” mean?
o: a last confession made to a monk just before you die
a funeral rite held for the family after a death
chanting the name with the dying, so no one is alone

games.q: the name at the end: tap the pairs.
p: tells the dying man to say the name

s: in helping recitation, people take turns so the name never stops
the dying person can follow it with their mind even without breath to say it.
every Pure Land school treats the last hour as the decisive test
for Shinran, birth is settled when shinjin is given, so the last hour is not a test.
deathbed practice depends only on what the dying person can do
it grows from the good friend at the bedside: who is sitting with them matters.

games.q: your grandmother is dying and can no longer speak. her temple friends begin chanting the name around the bed. what does helping recitation ask of you?
o: stay silent so she can rest.
take a turn, so the name never stops.
games.why: in zhunian, people take turns chanting, so the dying person can follow the name with their mind to the end.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is ill, or old, or near the end, or someone who has already died; if no one comes, hold a stranger in a hospital bed tonight.
Picture them resting in a soft, wide light, the way Pure Land Buddhists picture the light of Amitabha. If you say the name, say it for them quietly; if not, just keep them company in your mind.
And if a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, you don't have to: in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help where you are.

wordCard.voice: At the end of life. Pure Land practice at the deathbed: the name said with the dying, so no one meets the dark alone. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the name at the end. Be gentle with yourself tonight.
